title: Classes that keep their data valid
objectives: Write a class whose constructor and methods protect an invariant.
Keep data private, check every change, and mark readers `const`.

screens.title: Nothing stops a struct
screens.question: What does the last line print?

options.text: A compile error, because the bid is now above the ask
options.why: You expected the compiler to know the rule. It checks types only, and 100.6 is a valid `double`.
You used the old bid. The line before set `q.bid` to 100.6, so the ask minus the bid is negative.

options.text: The program stops when it runs

The assignment changed this cell.
The ask is 100.4 and the bid is now 100.6: 100.4 − 100.6.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow `q.bid` through each line.

byKey.compile: You expected the compiler to know the rule. It checks types only, and 100.6 is a valid `double`.

explain.text: Every member of a `struct` is open to any code, as in Python. The typo made a quote whose bid is above its ask, and it printed a negative spread. Nothing in the language knew the rule.

canvas.caption: The bid is above the ask: a crossed quote.

screens.title: Who may touch what
screens.prose: Suppose a type could hide some members from outside code. Here are the members of a better `Quote`. `set_bid(b)` checks `b` against the ask before it stores it.
screens.question: Drag each member into a box so that no code outside `Quote` can cross the quote.

hints.text: Which members, if anyone could write them, would let outside code skip the check?
These two hold the numbers the rule is about.
Hide `bid_` and `ask_`. Leave the three functions open: two only read, and `set_bid` checks.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask of each member: could outside code break the rule through it?

byKey.bid: If any code can write `bid_`, it can set 100.6 and skip every check. Keep it where only `Quote`'s functions reach it.
byKey.ask: If any code can write `ask_`, it can drop it below the bid. Keep it where only `Quote`'s functions reach it.
byKey.mid: `mid()` only reads. Hiding it protects nothing and stops everyone from using the quote.
byKey.spread: `spread()` only reads. Hiding it protects nothing and stops everyone from using the quote.
byKey.setbid: `set_bid` checks before it stores, so outside code may call it. Hidden, nobody could ever move the bid.

explain.text: You hid the data and left open the functions that read or check. C++ calls the hidden part **private** and the open part **public**. Outside code can then change the bid only through `set_bid`, which checks.

screens.title: private, checked by the compiler
screens.prose: Here is that split in C++. A **class** marks its sections `public:` and `private:`. A `struct` is the same thing, except its members are public until you say otherwise. Outside code then writes the bid directly.

params.title: main.cpp
lines: Quote(double bid, double ask) : bid_(bid), ask_(ask) {}

params.title: Terminal
lines: main.cpp:12:7: error: 'bid_' is a private member of 'Quote'

screens.question: What did the compiler refuse?

options.text: Code outside the class writing a private member
Storing a bid above the ask
options.why: You expected a check on the value. The compiler refused the name `bid_` before looking at any number.
The sections can come in any order. The error line names a private member.
Both are allowed. The error is about who may name `bid_`.

hints.text: Read the first `error:` line in the terminal.
It names the member and the class.
`'bid_' is a private member of 'Quote'`: line 12 is outside the class, so it may not name `bid_`.

feedback.correct: The rule is about names: outside code may not name `bid_`.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the `error:` line word by word.

byKey.value: You expected a check on the value. The compiler refused the name `bid_` before looking at any number.

explain.text: Line 12 is in `main`, outside `Quote`, so it may not name a private member. Python has no such check: `q._bid = 100.6` runs, because the underscore is only a convention. C++ refuses before the program even exists.

screens.title: A checked constructor
screens.prose: Now write the class. The **initialiser list**, `: bid_(bid), ask_(ask)`, builds each member before the body runs. The body then checks the rule. A bid equal to the ask is refused too: a zero spread is a locked quote. `const` after `mid()` promises the function only reads.

lines: Quote(100.0, 100.0)   // stops: bid not below ask
Quote(101.0, 100.0)   // stops: bid not below ask
params.title: What it should do

screens.question: Write the constructor's check, `double mid() const` and `double spread() const`. A failed check may `throw` or call `std::abort()`.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB), and the first compile takes 10 to 15 s; later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Check runs 6 hidden tests. Doubles are accepted within a relative 1e-9. Two tests build a bad quote and pass only if the program stops: a `throw` ends it here, because this browser build cannot catch exceptions.

hints.text: Put the check in the constructor's body, after the list has built the members.
A locked quote, bid equal to ask, must stop the program too.
`if (bid_ >= ask_) throw std::invalid_argument("bid must be below ask");` then `double mid() const { return (bid_ + ask_) / 2; }`.

feedback.correct: Every `Quote` that exists now has its bid below its ask.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test under the editor.

byKey.compile: The compiler stopped. If the message says a function is not marked const, add `const` after its brackets. If it names `mid` or `spread`, the function is missing.
byKey.test-4: Test 4 builds a quote with the bid above the ask, and your program carried on. Check in the constructor body.
byKey.test-5: Test 5 builds a quote with the bid equal to the ask. Refuse it too: use `>=` in the check, not `>`.

explain.text:
The list builds `bid_` and `ask_`; the body refuses a crossed or locked quote before anyone can use it. `mid` and `spread` are `const`, so they work on a `const Quote&` too. Inside them `bid_` means `this->bid_`, where `this` points at the object the function was called on.

```cpp
if (bid_ >= ask_) throw std::invalid_argument("bid must be below ask");
```

screens.title: Two numbers that move together
screens.prose: A `Position` holds a quantity of shares and their **average price**. You hold 100 shares bought at £10.00, then buy 300 more at £12.00.
screens.question: What is the average price of the 400 shares, in pounds?

hints.text: What did the 400 shares cost in total?
300 of the 400 shares cost £12.00 each.
Total cost $100 \times 10 + 300 \times 12 = 4600$, over 400 shares.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the total cost by the total shares.

byKey.simple: You averaged the two prices. Three times as many shares were bought at £12.00, so they pull the average up.
byKey.last: That is the price of the last buy. The first 100 shares still cost £10.00.

explain.text: You weighted each price by its shares: $4600 / 400 = 11.5$. The quantity and the average change together on every buy. A class can make sure they never drift apart.

screens.title: buy and sell
screens.prose: Now let the class keep the two numbers consistent. A buy moves the average; a sale does not. This desk forbids going short, so a sale above the holding is refused. A **flat** position, with no shares, has average price 0.
screens.question: Write `buy(int qty, double px)` and `sell(int qty)` to match the table. Refuse a buy of 0 or fewer shares, and any sale above the holding.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB), and the first compile takes 10 to 15 s; later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Check runs 10 hidden tests, each a short sequence of buys and sells. Prices are accepted within a relative 1e-9. Three tests pass only if the program stops.

hints.text: Update the average before you add to `qty_`: the formula needs the old quantity.
The last row sells 1 share of none.
`avg_ = (qty_ * avg_ + qty * px) / (qty_ + qty); qty_ += qty;` In `sell`, check, subtract, and reset `avg_` when `qty_` is 0.

feedback.correct: Quantity and average now move together, and never go short.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test under the editor.

byKey.test-2: Test 2 expects £11.50. Weight each price by its shares, and use `qty_` before you add the new shares.
byKey.test-4: Test 4 sells 150 shares and expects the average to stay £11.50. A sale changes only the quantity.
byKey.test-6: Test 6 sells everything. Set the average back to 0 when the quantity reaches 0.
byKey.test-8: Test 8 sells 101 of 100 shares. Refuse before you change `qty_`.
byKey.test-9: Test 9 buys 0 shares. Without a check the average becomes $0/0$, which is NaN.

explain.text: `buy` updates the average from the old quantity, then the quantity. `sell` refuses a short before changing anything, so a refused sale leaves the position as it was. The flat case resets the average, so no stale price survives.

screens.title: Build members in the list
screens.prose: A risk limit should never change once it is set, so its member is `const`. This constructor sets it in the body instead of the initialiser list.

params.title: Terminal
lines: main.cpp:3:5: error: constructor for 'Limit' must explicitly initialize the const member 'max_'
main.cpp:4:14: error: cannot assign to non-static data member 'max_' with const-qualified type 'const double'

screens.question: Which constructor compiles?

options.why: That is the code that failed. By the time the body runs, `max_` already exists, and a `const` cannot be assigned.
`this->max_` is the same member. It is still an assignment after the member was built.
That makes a new local variable that hides the member. The member is still never set, so the first error remains.

hints.text: When does the body of a constructor run: before or after the members exist?
The first error says the member must be explicitly initialised.
Members are built in the initialiser list, before the body. A `const` member can only get its value there.

feedback.correct: The list builds `max_` with its value, once.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A `const` member gets its value when it is built, in the list.

byKey.body: That is the code that failed. By the time the body runs, `max_` already exists, and a `const` cannot be assigned.

explain.text: The list builds each member with its value; the body runs after that. Assigning in the body builds the member first, then overwrites it, which a `const` forbids. Use the list for every member, not only `const` ones.

screens.title: One unchecked door
screens.prose: This `Quote` checks its constructor and keeps its data private. A colleague adds a setter.

lines: Quote(double bid, double ask) : bid_(bid), ask_(ask) {
double spread() const { return ask_ - bid_; }
params.title: main.cpp

screens.question: What does the program print?

options.text: Nothing: it stops, because the constructor checks the bid
options.why: You expected the constructor's check to guard every change. It runs once, when `q` is built; `set_bid` stores 100.6 without asking.

options.text: A compile error, because `bid_` is private
options.why: `set_bid` is a member function, so it may write `bid_`. Private stops outside code, not the class's own functions.
`set_bid` did store 100.6. The spread is 100.4 − 100.6.

hints.text: When does the constructor's check run?
This line changes `bid_`. Does it check anything?
The check ran once, on line 14. Line 15 calls `set_bid`, which stores 100.6 straight away.

feedback.correct: A private member is only as safe as the functions that write it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Trace line 15 into `set_bid`.

byKey.ctor: You expected the constructor's check to guard every change. It runs once, when `q` is built; `set_bid` stores 100.6 without asking.

screens.title: Invariants
screens.question: Which member function of `Quote` can safely skip the check?

options.why: It changes `ask_`, so it could drop the ask below the bid. It must check.

options.text: `void widen(double d)`, which subtracts `d` from the bid and adds it to the ask
options.why: With a negative `d` it narrows the quote and can cross it. It changes data, so it checks.
The constructor is the first place the rule can break. Every object passes through it.

hints.text: Which function cannot change `bid_` or `ask_` at all?
`const` after the brackets means the function cannot change the members, so the invariant still holds when it returns.

feedback.correct: A `const` function cannot change the members, so it cannot break the rule.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for the one function that cannot write to the members.

explain.text: `spread() const` only reads, so the invariant holds after it as before. Every other function on the list changes a member, so each must check. The compiler enforces `private` and `const`; the checks are yours.

screens.title: An order that cannot be filled twice
screens.prose: An order moves through states. It is `new` while it has shares left, even when partly filled, and `filled` when none remain. A cancel ends it. A filled or cancelled order accepts nothing more. Its state is an `enum class`, a type with named values.
screens.question: Write the constructor's check (quantity above 0), `fill(int q)` and `cancel()`. Refuse a fill or cancel on an order that is not `new`, a fill of 0 or fewer, and any fill beyond what remains.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB), and the first compile takes 10 to 15 s; later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Check runs 11 hidden tests, each a short sequence of fills and cancels. Five pass only if the program stops.

hints.text: Each function that changes the order checks its state first.
Only `new` has arrows leaving it.
In `fill`: refuse unless `state_ == State::New`, refuse `q <= 0` or `filled_ + q > qty_`, add, then set `State::Filled` when `filled_ == qty_`.

feedback.correct: The order's states only move along the arrows.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test under the editor.

byKey.test-4: Test 4 fills 40 then 60 of 100 and expects `filled`. Change the state when nothing remains.
byKey.test-7: Test 7 fills a cancelled order. Check the state before you add to `filled_`.
byKey.test-8: Test 8 fills 70 then 40 of 100. Refuse a fill larger than what remains.
byKey.test-9: Test 9 cancels a filled order. `cancel` must check the state too.

explain.text: Each changing function checks the state first, so the only moves are the arrows from `new`. The fill check also keeps `filled_` between 0 and the order size. An exchange gateway relies on exactly this: a late fill on a cancelled order is a real event, and it must be caught, not booked.

ideas: A `class` keeps its data `private`, so only its own member functions can change it. Python's `_name` is only a convention; C++ checks at compile time.
An invariant is checked in the constructor and again in every function that changes the data. Functions that only read are marked `const`.
Members are built in the initialiser list, before the constructor's body runs. A `const` member can only get its value there.

formula.name: Weighted average price
formula.note: A buy of $q_b$ shares at $p_b$ moves the average; a sale changes only $q$.

summary.trap: A setter that stores without checking, or a getter that returns a non-const reference, lets outside code break the invariant the constructor checked.

quiz.question: What happens?

options.text: A compile error: you cannot assign to a function call
options.why: `bid()` returns a `double&`, another name for `bid_` itself. Assigning to it compiles and writes the private member.

options.text: It stops, because the constructor checks the bid
options.why: The constructor checked once, when `q` was built. The reference writes `bid_` with no check.

options.text: It prints `0.2`, because `bid()` hands out a copy
options.why: A copy would need the return type `double`. With `double&` the caller writes the member itself.

feedback.correct: A non-const reference is an open door to private data.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the return type of `bid()`.

explain.text: `double& bid()` returns a reference to the private member, so `q.bid() = 100.6` writes it directly. Return `double`, or `const double&`, and that line no longer compiles.

quiz.prose:
The same class in Python, with the usual underscore for private data:

```python
class Quote:
    def __init__(self, bid, ask):
        if not bid < ask:
            raise ValueError("crossed")
        self._bid, self._ask = bid, ask

q = Quote(100.2, 100.4)
q._bid = 100.6
print(q._ask - q._bid)
```
quiz.question: What happens?

options.why: The underscore is a convention for readers. Python lets any code write `q._bid`.
`__init__` checked once, when `q` was built. The assignment afterwards runs no check.
Python prints a float's full shortest repr, so the binary error shows: `-0.19999999999998863`.

feedback.correct: Python trusts the caller; C++ `private` does not.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Python has no access check at all.

explain.text: In Python `_bid` only signals "leave this alone"; the assignment runs. C++ `private` is checked by the compiler, so the same line would not build.

quiz.question: What is the right fix?

options.why: That compiles, but now `width` could change the quote, and it can no longer take a `const Quote`.
The error is about a promise not to change the object, not about access.
That compiles by copying the quote on every call. The real gap is that `spread` never promised to only read.

feedback.correct: A reader should say it only reads.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The message says the function is not marked const.

explain.text: A `const Quote&` may call only `const` functions, since only they promise not to change it. `spread` only reads, so marking it `const` is honest and fixes every caller at once.

quiz.prose: A position holds 200 shares at £5.00. You buy 50 at £6.00, then sell 100.
quiz.question: What is the average price after the sale, in pounds?

feedback.correct: £1,300 over 250 shares is £5.20, and selling leaves it there.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight the two buys by their shares; the sale changes only the quantity.

byKey.simple: You averaged £5.00 and £6.00. Four times as many shares cost £5.00.
byKey.sold: That is the last buy's price. The average covers all 250 shares bought.

explain.text: The buys give $(1000 + 300) / 250 = 5.2$. Selling 100 shares leaves 150 at the same average cost, £5.20.
